text.p: The price of lead fell on Monday to its lowest for more than a year amid reports in the market of persistent selling by China.
Lead fell as low at $666 per tonne on the London Metal Exchange (LME), a 13-month low, down from Friday's close at $680.
Traders said the move came against a backdrop of rising warehouse stocks

"The market has been drifting lower over the last few months...there is no real reason behind the move," one trader commented, adding he believed the market had the potential to fall further by year-end.
There have been reports of persistent sales by China, which have overburdened the physical market.
In the first eight months of this year, Chinese exports of refined lead to the West totalled 145,000 tonnes, against 143,000 tonnes for the whole of 1995.
LME lead stocks stand at 122,675 tonnes, a rise of over 40 percent from March 1996 levels of 87,000 tonnes.
Among the other industrial metals, copper consolidated after last week's losses but tin extended a decline to ease to its softest levels in a month. It slid to $5,855 per tonne in late London.

Precious metal prices eased amid a renewed bearish sentiment. Gold closed in London $368.95 against the close of $369.65 on Friday when prices had bounced after comments by U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan.

Greenspan said investors should be wary of "irrational exuberance" in asset markets, prompting a short-lived sell-off in equities that led to short covering in bullion in case "hot" money sought a safe haven there. "It's very disappointing that all the markets turned around after a real burst to the upside on Friday, especially gold, which has really given up the ghost," a dealer said.
Traders said soft commodity markets were likely to ease this week, mainly because of an absence of buyers and a bearish technical outlook.
They said cocoa would continue to watch the gyrations of sterling while the fundamental picture was mixed, adding that the main snag seemed to be a lack of industry buyers.
London cocoa extended losses on long liquidation after sterling calmed down with March ending 12 pounds sterling lower at 934 sterling.
Traders said white sugar futures backed off earlier highs in a listless Monday session as the London market kept pace with the slight weakness in the New York raws.

The spot March contract briefly nudged up to $300 resistance before the New York open but a disappointing performance on the raws prompted commission house selling in London to erase the earlier strength seen from trade purchases.

Oil prices eased after U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali approved the start of an oil-for-food deal with Iraq which would enable Baghdad to return to the world oil market for the first time since 1990.

The deal will allow Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months, on a renewable basis to buy food, medicine and other humanitarian goods to alleviate the effects of sanctions imposed since the country's 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
The deal will come into force early on Tuesday.
Benchmark Brent Blend crude from the North Sea fell just
below $24 per barrel.
